extracted.intended_audience: USCIS adjudicators, immigration practitioners, and public commenters on the proposed public‑charge rule
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether an alien is likely to become a public charge under DHS's proposed public‑charge regulation using a forward‑looking 'totality of the circumstances' test. The rubric lists mandatory factors, evidentiary expectations, weighting rules, and examples from administrative case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality of the circumstances standard
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes to codify the totality of the circumstances standard: an alien’s age; health; family status; assets, resources, and financial status; and education and skills. In the Government’s discretion, the determination can also account for an affidavit of support filed under section 213A. DHS’s proposed totality of the circumstances standard would involve weighing all the positive and negative considerations related to an alien’s age; health; family status; assets, resources, and financial status; education and skills; required affidavit of support; and any other factor or circumstance that may warrant consideration in the public charge inadmissibility determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forward‑looking analysis considering all factors bearing on ability to be self‑supporting. If negative factors outweigh positive factors, alien found likely to become a public charge; if positive factors outweigh negative factors, alien not found likely to become a public charge. The agency should consider the totality of circumstances as developed in administrative case law and no single factor is outcome‑determinative absent statutory or regulatory instruction. Positive factors are those that decrease likelihood of becoming a public charge; negative factors increase that likelihood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age (mandatory factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: An alien’s age is a mandatory factor that must be considered when determining whether an alien is likely to become a public charge in the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS proposes to assess whether the alien is between 18 and the minimum 'early retirement age' for social security purposes (61 as of 2017). DHS would consider a person’s age between 18 and 61 as a positive factor, and consider a person’s age under 18 or over 61 to be a negative factor when determining likelihood of becoming a public charge. Age is considered primarily in relation to employment or employability, and secondarily as relevant to other factors. DHS acknowledges exceptions (e.g., persons under 18 or over 61 may be working or have adequate means of support and such means would be recognized as positive factors). Relevant statutory references: INA section 212(a)(4)(B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Health (mandatory factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: An alien’s health is a factor that must be considered when determining whether an alien is likely to become public charge in the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the alien has any physical or mental condition that, although not rendering the alien inadmissible under health‑related inadmissibility ground, is significant enough to interfere with ability to care for self, to attend school or work, or is likely to require extensive medical treatment or institutionalization in the future. Consider private health insurance or financial resources to pay medical costs as part of assets/resources. The mere presence of a medical condition is not determinative; DHS weighs the effect of the condition on ability to work or be self‑supporting in the totality analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family status
rubrics_metrics.description: Family status is among the enumerated factors to consider under the totality of the circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Family status includes consideration of spouse, parents, dependents, and the availability of friends/relatives in the United States who are willing and able to provide assistance. Case law has given positive weight where friends or relatives in the United States have indicated ability/willingness to assist; family resources and household members' income may also be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assets, resources, and financial status
rubrics_metrics.description: An alien’s assets, resources, and financial status (including sufficiency of funds for self‑support) are an enumerated factor to consider.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS notes assets/resources often carry considerable positive weight because they are the most tangible factors. Assets/resources include income, savings, investments, trust funds, Social Security benefits, Medicare, employer pensions, and other resources. Assets/resources examined together may outweigh concerns about age, education, skills, or health; conversely, limited assets/resources may require positive attributes in other factors to avoid a finding of likely public charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and skills
rubrics_metrics.description: An alien’s education and skills are an enumerated factor in the totality analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education and skills inform employability and future earnings potential. They are weighed with other factors (age, health, work history, etc.) to assess ability to be self‑supporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit of support / sponsorship (section 213A / Form I‑864)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Government’s discretion, the determination can account for an affidavit of support filed under section 213A of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1183a.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS would give positive weight to a Form I‑864 that satisfies statutory and regulatory requirements and to income/resources of certain household members, but the filing of Form I‑864 and shared resources are not determinative. The adequacy (or absence/insufficiency) of an affidavit of support is a factor but does not alone determine the outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to earn a living / employment factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability of the alien to earn a living, as evidenced or impacted by the alien’s age, health, work history, current employment status, future employment prospects, and skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law and DHS analysis consider vocation, past record of employment, current employment, offer of employment, and prospects for future employment. Ability to earn a living is a primary consideration because it directly affects self‑support and likelihood of requiring public benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to remedy current dependence on public benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability of the alien to remedy any current dependence on public benefits in the United States, as evidenced or impacted by the alien’s age, health, ability to earn a living, funds, and sponsorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS evaluates whether current reliance on benefits reflects a long‑term likelihood of dependence or whether other factors indicate capacity to become self‑supporting (e.g., employment prospects, sponsorship, assets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Past or current receipt of public benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Past or current receipt of public benefits is a factor but 'the fact that an alien has been on welfare does not, by itself, establish that he or she is likely to become a public charge.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS reiterates administrative precedent (Matter of Perez) that receipt of welfare alone is insufficient to sustain a finding of likely public charge; it must be evaluated within the totality of circumstances alongside other factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighting and determinative rules
rubrics_metrics.description: No single factor or circumstance that Congress mandated DHS to consider, or which DHS may otherwise determine to consider, would determine the outcome of a public charge inadmissibility determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some factors and circumstances would generally carry heavy weight (DHS identifies assets/resources as frequently carrying considerable positive weight). The weight given to an individual factor not designated as carrying heavy weight depends on facts and the relationship of the factor to other factors. Multiple factors operating together may be weighed more heavily. DHS also explains that 'any factor or circumstance that decreases the likelihood of an applicant becoming a public charge is positive; any factor or circumstance that increases the likelihood ... is negative.' The agency will conclude inadmissible if specific negative factors outweigh positive ones and not inadmissible if positives outweigh negatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: USCIS evidentiary requirements for the health factor
rubrics_metrics.description: USCIS' review of the health factor would include, but not be limited to, consideration of: (1) any required Report of Medical Examination and Vaccination Record (Form I‑693) or applicable DOS medical examination form submitted in support of the application for the diagnosis of any medical conditions; or (2) evidence of a medical condition that is likely to require extensive medical treatment or institutionalization after arrival, or that will interfere with the alien’s ability to care for him‑ or herself, to attend school, or to work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference to Form I‑693 (or DOS equivalent) is intended to standardize assessment and avoid multiple medical exams. Most immigrant visa applicants and adjustment applicants are required to submit a medical exam; nonimmigrants generally are not, except in specified cases. A consular officer or CBP officer may request an exam where health inadmissibility is a concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class A and Class B medical conditions and physician reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Class A medical conditions (communicable disease of public health significance, failure to meet vaccination requirements, present/past physical or mental disorders with associated harmful behavior, drug abuse/addiction) make an alien inadmissible on health‑related grounds; Class B medical conditions are physical or mental conditions serious in degree or permanent in nature and, while not rendering an alien inadmissible on health grounds, are relevant to the public charge determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physicians conducting immigration medical exams are directed to explain on the medical report 'the nature and extent of the abnormality; the degree to which the alien is incapable of normal physical activity; and the extent to which the condition is remediable ... [and] the likelihood, that because of the condition, the applicant will require extensive medical care or institutionalization.' A waiver of the health‑related ground of inadmissibility is available for certain Class A conditions; nonetheless, Class A/B findings may be considered in the public charge analysis as part of the health factor.
